clinicalPearls: One of the RASopathies, overlapping clinically with Noonan and Costello syndromes but generally with more marked ectodermal and neurodevelopmental involvement
The face is relatively coarse with a high forehead, bitemporal narrowing, down-slanting palpebral fissures, ptosis and low-set posteriorly rotated ears
Ectodermal features are prominent: sparse curly hair, absent or sparse eyebrows and eyelashes, keratosis pilaris, ichthyosis and multiple naevi
Congenital heart disease, especially pulmonary valve stenosis, atrial septal defect and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, is common
Caused by activating variants in the RAS-MAPK pathway, most often BRAF, then MAP2K1/MAP2K2 and less commonly KRAS
Feeding difficulty with failure to thrive and gastro-oesophageal reflux is frequent and often severe in infancy
Intellectual disability is usually moderate to severe, more so than in classic Noonan syndrome, and seizures are common
reference.pathophysiology: Cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome is a RASopathy caused by germline activating variants in components of the RAS-MAPK (mitogen-activated protein kinase) signalling cascade, principally BRAF and the downstream kinases MEK1 and MEK2, with a minority in KRAS. This pathway transduces growth-factor signals to control cell proliferation, differentiation and survival. Constitutive over-activation dysregulates these processes during development, producing the characteristic craniofacial, cardiac, ectodermal and neurodevelopmental abnormalities shared, with variation, across the RASopathy spectrum.
additionalDifferentials: Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines (LEOPARD syndrome)
additionalInvestigations: Gene-panel or exome sequencing of the RAS-MAPK pathway, including BRAF, MAP2K1, MAP2K2 and KRAS
Echocardiography for pulmonary stenosis, septal defects and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Electroencephalography and brain MRI for seizures and structural anomalies
Growth and nutritional assessment, with feeding evaluation for reflux
Ophthalmology review for ptosis, strabismus and refractive error
Dermatological assessment of the ectodermal findings
redFlags: Signs of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia causing cardiac compromise
Failure to thrive and dehydration from severe feeding difficulty
Rapidly changing or atypical skin lesions warranting review
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends heavily on the cardiac phenotype, particularly hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and on the severity of feeding and neurological problems; many individuals have moderate to severe intellectual disability. With multidisciplinary care most survive into adulthood, though medical needs remain substantial.
pitfalls: Confusing it with Noonan or Costello syndrome, which alters cancer surveillance and prognosis
Underestimating early feeding failure and delaying nutritional support
Overlooking hypertrophic cardiomyopathy that can progress silently
Assuming skin and hair findings are an unrelated ectodermal disorder
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Provide supportive, manifestation-directed care, as there is no disease-modifying therapy for the underlying RAS-MAPK dysregulation
Manage congenital heart disease with balloon valvuloplasty for pulmonary valve stenosis and surveillance and treatment of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Address feeding difficulty and failure to thrive with nutritional support, nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding and treatment of gastro-oesophageal reflux
Control seizures with anticonvulsant therapy and monitor neurodevelopment
Provide developmental support with physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy and educational input
Treat the ectodermal features and offer ophthalmology review for ptosis, strabismus and refractive error
Coordinate multidisciplinary care and offer genetic counselling, noting most variants arise de novo
